answer_en:
DataForSEO (DFS) is used for one thing: measuring what travellers actually type into Google about the places on our itineraries. It answers three questions. How many searches a month a phrase gets, from the search_volume endpoint. Which related phrases people use, from keywords_for_keywords. Which "People Also Ask" questions and which ranking websites show up for a phrase, from serp_advanced. The answers are cached in acp_contract.search_demand (one row per keyword and market, holding volume, people_also_ask and serp_domains). acp_contract.segment_research_log records each (place, market) pair researched, and a pair counts as fresh for 182 days. A second, per-tour cache, silver_aa_internal.seo_context, holds the S1/A1 keyword ideas and the tour-level PAA.

A "market" is just the buyer country the search numbers come from. The code supports six (US 2840, UK 2826, AU 2036, DE 2276, FR 2250, NL 2528, in DFS_LOCATION_MAP). The markets come from a tenant's target_market.countries, with US as the fallback. In admin research, the admin types them in explicitly. Because DFS bills each keyword lookup once per market, the same keyword in 3 markets costs about 3 times as much. That is why the 25/09 run (US, UK and AU) was expensive.

Nothing downstream calls DFS. Every consumer only reads the caches:
- **Ranking (Score).** search_demand feeds the demand axis and the PAA-landing questions axis of atom_ranking. A Segment with no measured demand takes the median demand rank, so it is neither blocked nor zeroed.
- **Blog Bar in the Slate.** Blog needs demand ≥ 1000 and questions ≥ 3. Missing demand is read as 0, so the Segment silently fails the Bar and never becomes a Blog Subject. The social Channels and Email/Landing/Ads do not use demand at all.
- **T8 angles.** The search-demand/PAA block is simply left out of the prompt when there is no data.
- **T9 blog FAQ.** It reads real questions from the DB through a chain (Segment matches, place PAA, admin top-up, tour PAA). With none, the writer makes up its own FAQ questions, labelled 'writer'.
- **T2 tenant rewrite.** It reads the tenant-market keywords from search_demand, falls back to the US seo_context row, and otherwise writes with no keywords.
- **S1/A1 rewrite.** This admin path does buy DFS per tour through process_seo / s1_seo_prefetch. It reuses a tour's row for 180 days and writes without SEO if the budget stops it.

To answer your question directly: no, a tenant writing a blog does not re-run DFS today. Until 28/09 (AA-646), every tenant T2 rewrite (a tour rewrite, not a blog) launched research over every place on the platform. That one run on 25/09 covered 2,215 places × 3 markets and cost $49.02. Since commit d3921934b (29/09), research runs only when an admin starts it, capped at 200 places per run. The T2/T8/T9/Slate paths only read the DB, and a unit test blocks the paid deep-SERP call from every path except the admin script.

answer_en:
I recommend one full research pass per market, platform-wide, before any per-tenant scheme. Buy only search volumes, in near-full 1000-keyword tasks. Buy the People-Also-Ask SERP only for places whose volume clears the Blog demand bar. Stop buying keywords_for_keywords for segment research. Estimated cost: about 4 USD of DataForSEO (DFS) for the US (about 2.7 volumes + about 1.3 SERP), about 3.4 each for UK and AU, plus about 3.4 USD of Haiku once for keyword proposals. That is about 14 USD for all three markets. The AA-1055 plan as written is about 60 USD for the US alone.

Where the 60 USD comes from: the run estimate (segment_research_batch.py:131-147) for 200 places is 1 volume task (0.09) + 200 SERPs (0.40) + 10 keywords_for_keywords tasks (0.90) + Haiku (0.28), about 1.67 USD. So keywords_for_keywords is about 65% of the DFS spend and SERP about 29%. Volumes are only 6%. The 200-place cap (admin_segment_research.py:45) barely hurts volume cost: 800 keywords still fit one task. Its real cost is about 36 separate approvals per market.

Option 1, full batch: 7,323 places × 4 keywords is about 29,300 keywords, so 30 tasks × 0.09 = 2.7 USD per market (1.35 with only the 2 fixed keywords per place). SERP only at volume ≥1000 is roughly 9% of places in the US, 4-5% in UK/AU, so about 0.6-1.3 USD per market. The share comes from the search_demand cache, keyword rows as a proxy, not verified per place.

Option 2, only places on tours tenants use: the audit tenant's 14 tours are 176 places, about 1.34 USD with keywords_for_keywords and about 0.2 without. The cache is already shared across tenants: search_demand is keyed by (keyword, market) with no tenant column. But once Option 1 costs about 4 USD per market, on-demand research only makes sense as the follow-up queue for new places.

Option 3, refresh and renames: FRESH_FOR is already 182 days, and Google Ads volumes are 12-month averages, so refresh every 6-12 months. That is about 8 USD per market per year, plus a weekly batched run for new places at about 0.09 USD per market per run. Today a rename turns the place stale, because segment_research_log is keyed by canonical_place, and the SERP is always bought live with no cache check. Reuse old research through alias cards and skip the SERP when PAA is already cached and fresh.

Option 4: drop keywords_for_keywords from segment research (use_suggestions=False; the flag already exists). Instead add '<place> <country>' as a second keyword in the same volume task, which costs nothing extra. Ms. Thư's reference config priced 'suggestions' at 0.0144 USD per request. AA-CIS uses Google Ads keywords_for_keywords at about 0.084-0.09. I could not check which endpoint her repo uses (it is not reachable).

Option 5: Google Ads Keyword Planner API is free but needs an Ads account, a developer token approved for Basic access, and OAuth. Accounts without ad spend reportedly get ranges such as 1K-10K, which is still enough for a ≥1000 test. It has no PAA. That is a lot of setup to save about 3 USD per market, so not now.

Option 6: the 1000-search Blog bar is copied literally from Ms. Thư's channels.toml, built for a dense Japan catalogue. Only 178 of 785 US keywords with volume reach 1000, so for niche Asian trekking places it will stay thin. A per-tenant or relative bar (for example top quartile with a floor of 100-200) is a product decision for Nghiệp; test it by replaying the audit tenant.

To the user's direct question: tenant blog writing does not buy DFS. Since AA-646 it only reads the cache. The big spends were the 25/09 sweep, when every T2 rewrite researched all platform places across 3 markets with about 4.5 keywords per paid task (49 USD), and the October S1 catalogue-rewrite SEO prefetch under the AA-internal tenant id, not real tenants.

answer_en:
No. As of CIS HEAD 8f6f53c1 (08/11/2026), nothing a tenant does buys DataForSEO. That covers T2 rewrite, T7 slate, T8 angles, T9 blog write and A3 export. They only read data that was already bought: the tables acp_contract.search_demand, silver_aa_internal.seo_context and acp_contract.atom_ranking.

Only three kinds of path can still make a paid DFS call, and an admin starts every one of them:
(1) Segment research: POST /admin/segment-research/run, then the segment_research job. It needs the admin secret and a max_places cap, runs one at a time, has a per-run budget and checks the balance first.
(2) The S1 (A1) rewrite of AA's own catalogue: /admin/run-tour, run-tour-async, the s1_rewrite job, s1-batch and the s1_seo_prefetch job. All of these call process_seo or prefetch.
(3) The AA-779 SERP question top-up. It runs only from scripts/aa779_serp_topup.py, with a $3 lifetime cap. The free balance check (appendix_user_data, $0) also goes through the same client.

The ledger rows tagged with a tenant (1035 calls, $19.49) come from path (2), not from a tenant action. Their cost adds up exactly from 21/09 ($0.91) plus 01/10–08/10 ($18.58). Those October days match the a1_seo LLM stage window (01/10–08/10) and the AA-653 prefetch going live on 01/10. Both S1 paths stamp tenant_id = AA internal (00000000-...-0001) by default, so these are AA's own catalogue rewrites carrying the AA tenant ID. The ledger aggregate does not show which tenant ID, so 'AA internal' is likely but not verified.

That path still exists. Since 31/10 (commit 3cfba249) process_seo runs under a $0.50 per-tour budget (dfs / job:s1_rewrite) and stops at it. Before 31/10 process_seo had no budget at all, so the October S1 spend ran outside cost_guard. The prefetch job has had a budget since 01/10.

The real 'tenant action buys DFS' bug was the 25/09 spike ($49.02, 1169 calls). It was logged as platform-wide (tenants=0) because segment_research never passed tenant_id to the client. Before commit b0dd9bea1 (28/09, AA-646), the tenant T2 rewrite endpoint in v1_tours.py fired run_segment_research for the tenant's markets in the background. After AA-545 made Segments platform-wide, that swept every platform place × AU/US/UK.

AA-646 removed that trigger on 28/09. On 29/09 (d3921934b) the last remaining tenant path closed: T2 used to call process_seo (about $0.18 per tour) when a tour had no seo_context row; now T2 only reads.

Answer for a tenant blog: T7 offers a Blog subject only when the Segment already has demand ≥1000 and ≥3 questions in atom_ranking, which is filled by earlier admin research. T8 and T9 read seo_context and search_demand. When that data is stale or missing, the blog gets fewer proposals or questions. It never triggers a new purchase.

One gap: there is no general static test that blocks tenant routes from importing DataForSEOClient. Only the T2 path (test_aa646_t2_no_dfs) and the deep-SERP path (test_aa779_real_first) are guarded by tests.

answer_en:
Most of the spend comes from one bug and one design flaw, not from DataForSEO being expensive per tour. The ledger shows 71.49 USD in total. 49.02 USD of it (69%) was spent on a single day, 25/09.

1) What triggered 25/09. Until commit b0dd9bea (28/09), every tenant T2 rewrite started `_run_research_only()` → `run_segment_research()` in v1_tours.py. AA-545 had made Segments platform-wide, so that function's unfiltered `SELECT canonical_place ... FROM acp_contract.atom_segment` covered the whole platform. Each tenant click therefore researched about 2,215 places × AU/US/UK. The S196 WanderLux test rewrites fired it twice (bursts of 563 and 605 live calls).

2) Why each call bought so little. The old per-place ReAct loop ran 4 places at a time (CONCURRENCY=4) with a 5-second batching window (`_VolumeBatcher`). Its 678 search-volume tasks carried 4.5 keywords on average (max 13), at about 0.058 USD per task, which came to 39.24 USD. DataForSEO prices per task, and one task can carry up to 1,000 keywords. The Bhutan pilot (28/09) shows the real price curve: a 152-keyword task cost 0.09 USD, so roughly 0.0006 USD per keyword instead of about 0.013.

The loop also bought one `keywords_for_keywords` task per zero-volume place: 100 single-seed tasks × 0.09 = 9.00 USD. Tasks with 1, 2 or 4 obscure seeds were later shown to return only the seeds and no ideas, so that money bought almost nothing. SERP calls were cheap (0.84 USD). On top of the DataForSEO bill there were 7,856 Haiku calls (10.27 USD).

3) Per place, the cost was not unusual. The reference repo budgets about 0.10–0.12 USD per place, and our 25/09 run cost about 0.12 USD for each of the roughly 420 places it actually finished. The problem was scale: the whole platform, for 3 markets, on every tenant click. The balance hit -0.12 USD after only about 17% of the intended lookups had been bought.

4) The cache was poisoned, not saved. Once the money ran out, `fetch_volumes_bulk` swallowed the errors. 14,691 NULL volumes were stored and 1,795 places were marked fresh for 182 days with no data. The 28/09 repair deleted 16,311 search_demand rows and 5,859 research_log rows. Everything bought after 08:51 UTC that day was lost or had to be thrown away.

5) Full batching would have cost far less. For the same keywords bought on 25/09 (about 3,050 keyword-market pairs), full batching means about 3–6 volume tasks, roughly 0.3–0.5 USD instead of 39.24. The whole intended sweep (about 19k pairs) would have been about 21 tasks, roughly 1.9 USD. The batch rewrite (AA-648) proved this on Bhutan: 50 places × 3 markets for 0.55 USD, about 0.011 USD per place, 10 times cheaper. The DE/FR/NL run on 12/10 cost 0.70 USD.

6) The October days were a different path. Those days carry a tenant ID (probably AA-internal, through the `s1_seo_prefetch` job) and match the per-tour S1 catalogue rewrite wave. In total they sum to 19.49 USD, together with 21/09 (5 tours) and 02/10. That spend is mostly `keywords_for_keywords`: 205 tasks, 16.65 USD in October, about 10.9 seeds per task where the limit is 20. AA-653 cut S1 from about 0.18 USD per tour (5 tours on 21/09 = exactly 0.91 USD) to about 0.026 USD per tour. Packing tasks to the full 20 seeds would have saved roughly another 6–7 USD. 05/10 (73 tours, 5.79 USD) looks like the one-task-per-tour path; I have not verified that from the per-day endpoint split.

7) What the caches saved. The 7-day Redis cache for `process_seo` (AA-625) logged 114 cache hits, worth roughly 19–20 USD at the 0.18-per-tour price of the time. The research cache keeps one row per market by design, because DataForSEO accepts one location per task. So 3 markets means 3 times as many tasks; AU and UK together cost 27.0 USD of the total. With full batching that is 3 tasks, not 3 × 678.

8) Renamed places make old research useless. Freshness is tracked by the exact `canonical_place` text, and volumes by the exact keyword text. Re-atomize renames places: there were 8,578 orphan Segments after the S1 v2 rewrite. That fits 7,116 of the 7,323 US places now showing as stale, but I have not split renamed places from never-researched ones.

9) Was `keywords_for_keywords` per place needed? Mostly no. It only helped obscure places when about 20 '<place> <country>' seeds were sent in one task. That is now the batch default, with tasks of fewer than 5 seeds skipped.

10) Do tenant blogs re-run DataForSEO? Not since 28–29/09. AA-646 removed the tenant trigger. Since KAN-90, the T2 rewrite job only reads the cached seo_context. The SERP top-up for blog questions (`question_topup.py`) runs only when an admin starts it, with a 3 USD cap across all runs.

11) One warning about the remaining work. A batch run over the 7,116 stale US places has an upper-bound estimate of about 49 USD, and about 32 USD of that is `keywords_for_keywords` tasks. With suggestions turned off the upper bound is about 17 USD; realistically about 5–8 USD.

I could not reach the reference repo (aa-social-media): `gh search repos` does not find it, so it is private or named differently. Everything I say about it comes from the AA-515 step0b doc.

answer_en:
Ms. Thư's reference repo is not on GitHub (gh search found nothing, and the org has only our six repos). A full local copy sits in the CIS repo at apps/AA-CIS-App/docs/AI-gent-for automation works/aa-soscial-media-main/, and I read it directly.

How her design works. The unit of research is the place, not the Segment and not the trip. One ReAct loop runs per place, with every activity at that place handed to it. Each loop is capped at 4 steps, 8 keywords, 2 SERPs and 1 suggestions call. Places that are pure transit or that name nowhere in particular are skipped. The scope of one run is one workspace, meaning one country export. Her Japan figures: 24 trips, 581 distinct places, of which 368 were worth researching.

Her cost controls:
- Before any loop starts, every place name is priced in one volume request per market.
- Concurrent loops (16 workers) pool their volume asks into one request carrying up to 1,000 keywords, throttled to the account's rate limit.
- Anything bought within 182 days is reused from the cache.
- Places whose fingerprint has not changed are skipped.
- The run budget is $0.12 per place.
- Suggestions use the cheap DataForSEO Labs keyword_suggestions endpoint at about $0.0144.

She uses a fixed 3 markets (US/UK/AU) with every keyword fanned out to all three. Her coverage figure: matching keywords to Segments by name instead of by embedding lifted Segments with any demand from 14% to 45%. Her measured figures: a simulated 0.75 volume requests per place gives about $25 for a full 368-place Japan run, against $198 without pooling. A sample summary in her README shows a $3.21 run (9 volume requests, 1,487 SERPs). Her README also says research must be a deliberate purchase, never chained unattended behind another stage.

AA-CIS ported the same caps and the same 182-day cache. The big difference is scope and trigger. AA-545 (06/09) made Segments platform-wide, so the research scope became every place in the whole catalog. Until AA-646 (29/09), research also fired automatically after every tenant T2 rewrite. On 25/09 a single tenant rewrite swept about 2,215 places across 3 markets. It spent $49.02 in 1,169 calls and drained the balance from $49.87 to -$0.12. Today 7,323 US places are in scope, against her 368 per country.

Per-call efficiency was also worse in three ways:
- Volume tasks carried only 4.5 to 7.2 keywords each, against her up to 1,000. The cause: our loop runs only 4 concurrent places, has no place-name pre-pricing, and waits a fixed 5 seconds rather than until all loops are ready. The batch rewrite (AA-648, 28/09) fixed this later.
- Suggestions use Google Ads keywords_for_keywords at about $0.084 a call, against her $0.0144. That is about 6 times the price, and those 316 calls cost $26.8, about 37% of all DataForSEO spend.
- No transit or unnamed-place filter shows up in the research scope query.

In plain terms: one research run per place costs about the same in her design and ours. We paid more because we researched the entire catalog's places, the run was triggered without a person deciding to buy, and the efficiency gaps above added to it.

On whether a tenant blog re-runs DataForSEO: since 29/09 the code says no. T2 rewrites only read cached SEO data. Research and the question top-up are admin-only, the top-up capped at $3 in total. The October days tagged with a tenant (up to 412 tours on 08/10) are most likely the admin S1 SEO prefetch during master rewrite waves, not tenant blogs. I have not verified that.

Why the DataForSEO cache does not stop re-buying: segment_research_log is keyed by canonical_place, an LLM-worded string. The AA-653 clean rerun (early October) deleted and re-atomized atom_segment, while keeping search_demand and segment_research_log (clean-rerun.md table, commit bdd36a558). Keyword-level volumes in search_demand are still reused if the wording is identical. Plausible, not verified live.
